utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The Chamber received information that, and, of course, we do know that you announced yesterday, Ms. Edgerton, that you'd like to make submissions in relation to the list that was D1216, if I remember well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And I must say, after court yesterday, our team met to arrive at a position with respect to D1216, which changes the nature of what I might say to you today, so what I'd like to do is put that position on the record. Now, in fact, our position was referred to yesterday by Mr. Tieger when he spoke with Your Honours and indicating that the Prosecution felt that D1216 was insufficiently reliable for the Trial Chamber to ground any findings on, and that, Your Honour, was confirmed by cross-examination. Confronted with repeated examples of the list's errors and deficiencies, including missing biographical information, the fact that it contains the names of an unknown number of soldier, persons still alive, evidence of Serb perpetrators, the witness yesterday could only repeat that the list was preliminary, he had no idea when it was last updated, and the files needed to be completed, although 20 years had elapsed and the commission that was supposed to verify the information never did so and no longer exists. So the list, Your Honours, in the Prosecution's view, doesn't advance the case beyond what's never been at issue as we indicated ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please focus very much on admissibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In terms of admissibility, Your Honour, I'm very mindful that the document was admitted because, as I had indicated, an objection was not voiced at the precise time, but the difference between an admitted and unadmitted document is the weight that the Trial Chamber accords to it. So, Your Honours, given our position on the document and in view these factors I've just articulated, what I wanted to advise Your Honours is that we're not going to be seeking the special relief of reconsideration in these circumstances, but we consider that Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is argument rather. If you're not seeking the reconsideration then we have a decision that it was admitted and if you say the difference between an admitted and unadmitted document is the weight that the Trial Chamber accords to it, well, I do not see what weight we could accord to an unadmitted document. To an admitted document, of course, we have to consider what weight to give it - that's what we always do - against the totality of the evidence. Therefore, you're not seeking our reconsideration. You might argue about the probative value when the time is there to do so. Anything else in relation to admission?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then -- thank you, Ms. Edgerton. Is the Defence ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. The witness is Mladjen Kenjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kenjic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. The text is now handed out to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Mr. Kenjic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you adjust the microphone. Mr. Kenjic, you'll first be examined by Mr. Stojanovic. You find Mr. Stojanovic to your left. Mr. Stojanovic is counsel for Mr. Mladic. Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MLADJEN KENJIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you to slowly state for the transcript your name and surname.

utterances.speaker: MLADJEN KENJIC
utterances.text: Mladjen Kenjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kenjic, at one point in time, did you give a statement in writing to the Defence of General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We cannot hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, would you please come a bit closer to the microphone and speak clearly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. [Interpretation] Will this do?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have to ask the interpreters because I hear them but they should hear you. And I think they're nodding yes so ... and don't move too far away.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kenjic, now I'm going to ask you to focus on the screen in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And could we have 65 ter 1D01766 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you see the first page of the statement in front of you on the screen? Could you please just tell us --

utterances.speaker: MLADJEN KENJIC
utterances.text: On the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: On the right-hand side. Can you recognise the signature there?

utterances.speaker: MLADJEN KENJIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you please look at the last page of this document as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please be assisted. Could the last page of the document be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, sir, do you recognise the signature on this page?

utterances.speaker: MLADJEN KENJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Whose signature is that?

utterances.speaker: MLADJEN KENJIC
utterances.text: Mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you enter the date here in your own hand, the 3rd of August, 2014?

utterances.speaker: MLADJEN KENJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kenjic, yesterday during the proofing, did you have an opportunity to read your statement once again?

utterances.speaker: MLADJEN KENJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Today, in this courtroom, now that you've taken the solemn declaration to speak the truth, after having read this statement of yours, after you read it yesterday, can you confirm today before this Court that everything contained in it is truthful and that you would answer the same questions identically today?

utterances.speaker: MLADJEN KENJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to tender Mr. Kenjic's statement into evidence. 65 ter 1D01766.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D01766 receives exhibit number D1218, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, Your Honour, I would like to read a short summary of Witness Mladjen Kenjic's statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness Mladjen Kenjic, as a military conscript was mobilised on the 2nd of April, 1992 and started working as a driver. As the JNA left from Bosnia-Herzegovina, he was given a new war-time assignment in the Protection Regiment of the VRS as driver of the commander of the Main Staff of the VRS, General Mladic. He assumed that duty in May 1992 and he discharged these duties until 2002. In his statement, he speaks about his specific duties, about the way in which trips were organised, and how General Mladic toured the terrain, about the functioning of the team that escorted General Mladic as he carried out his tasks, about the system of communications that was available, and especially about the way in which they travelled and the route they took, the accommodation they had, and the duration of the trip to Belgrade and back. Further on, he says that from the 13th or 14th of July, 1995, he was at home on leave and upon his return to Crna Rijeka, he remembers that he was given the assignment to drive General Mladic to Belgrade. He states in detail what his specific duties were during those days where he drove him and where he escorted General Mladic, starting with meetings in the building of the Presidency at Andricev Venac, Dobanovci, the wedding where General Mladic was best man, to the military medical academy VMA, and finally the way and time they returned to Crna Rijeka. He asserts that he drove General Mladic to Han Pijesak and Crna Rijeka sometime in the afternoon hours after three nights spent in Belgrade and then he returned to his regular military tasks. Your Honours, this is a brief summary of the witness's statement and with your leave, I'd just like to put a few more questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed as you suggest.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please take a look at paragraph 11 of D1218.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kenjic, do take a look at paragraph 11 of your statement now. Among other things, you say in the last sentence on that page, in the B/C/S version: "As far as I can remember we headed for Serbia in a civilian Ford Taunus that did not have any special communications equipment." Please, to the best of your recollection, could you tell us which vehicles you drove during the war as you were driving or escorts General Mladic and, in particular, I'm asking you whether you can recall whether these vehicles had any kind of communications equipment.

utterances.speaker: MLADJEN KENJIC
utterances.text: I can say that we had several vehicles. For the most part, we used the Puch which is a military vehicle. We also have other vehicles. It was only in that Puch vehicle that there was a radio transmitter that we practically never used. As for other vehicles, there was no such equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In this civilian vehicle, the Ford Taunus that you refer to here as being the vehicle that you took to Belgrade on that occasion, did that vehicle have any kind of communications system or equipment?

utterances.speaker: MLADJEN KENJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You say also in paragraph 11, a bit before that, you say: "Sometime around noon on the day I returned, I was given a task to take General Mladic to Serbia because, as he personally told me during the trip, he was not able to go there by helicopter." Please, if you can, in view of this sentence that you have before you, he took the helicopter, he started the trip on a helicopter but had to land because of the fog and return to Crna Rijeka by hitch-hiking, did General Mladic explain any of this to you in detail? Why he was asking you to drive him? Why he couldn't take the helicopter? Did he tell you anything along these lines?

utterances.speaker: MLADJEN KENJIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. When we set out, he told me that he had first started his trip by helicopter and then he returned because he couldn't fly because of the fog and I think he said that he to hitch-hike and he was in a hurry because Milosevic had asked him to come to a meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I did not quite understand what you said. Who was it that invited him to a meeting?

utterances.speaker: MLADJEN KENJIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I think that he said that the president, President Milosevic asked him to come to a meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, listening to the witness I thought, haven't I read that? Last question is entirely in the -- who told him, helicopter, even the word "hitch-hiking" apparently is -- What's the reason to again put the same questions to which the witness has attested already? Would you refrain from being repetitious. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: During the trip, did you stop anywhere?

utterances.speaker: MLADJEN KENJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, to the best of your recollection, which road did you take from Han Pijesak to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MLADJEN KENJIC
utterances.text: The usual road we took when we went there when it was necessary.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We can no longer hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could you please come closer to the microphone again because the interpreters have difficulties hearing you. If you would just sit upright rather than leaning back, that would assist.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I see that the transcript does not reflect everything you said. Could you slowly state the route you took to Belgrade then.

utterances.speaker: MLADJEN KENJIC
utterances.text: Han Pijesak, Vlasenica, Milici, Zvornik, Sabac, Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember which bridge you crossed in Zvornik when you crossed the border?

utterances.speaker: MLADJEN KENJIC
utterances.text: Karakaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us please look at paragraph 12 of your statement now. This is what you say there in the second sentence so I'm talking about that first day in Belgrade. Milosevic, Andricev Venac and Dobanovci and then you say, that evening, late that evening we drove General Mladic home ..." Do tell us if you remember what time that could have been when you say: "Late that evening we drove General Mladic home"?

utterances.speaker: MLADJEN KENJIC
utterances.text: Well, in the evening. Now what time it was, I cannot say that precisely. Well, really it was very late. 10.00, 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kenjic, thank you for these answers. Thank you for your assistance. Those are the questions that we had for you at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I have a question for clarification. What date was this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When we arrived Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What was the date when you drove Mr. Milosevic in the evening at 10.00 -- sorry. When you drove Mr. Mladic from a meeting with Mr. Milosevic at 10.00 in the evening? When you drove him back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it was the 14th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stojanovic. Mr. McCloskey, are you ready to cross-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kenjic, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. McCloskey. You find Mr. McCloskey to your right. Mr. McCloskey is counsel for the Prosecution. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kenjic.

utterances.speaker: MLADJEN KENJIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In your statement that counsel just showed you, it's -- we see that it's dated 3 of August 2014. Can you tell us who wrote up that statement that you signed?

utterances.speaker: MLADJEN KENJIC
utterances.text: One of the lawyers, I think, Dundjer I think is his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did have you any additions or subtractions from the first draft that he showed you?

utterances.speaker: MLADJEN KENJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And were you able to review any prior statements you made to anyone before giving the Defence the statement?

utterances.speaker: MLADJEN KENJIC
utterances.text: I did not understand you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. You -- we see your statement is dated 3rd August 2014. Is that the time that you actually gave the statement to the Defence and signed it?

utterances.speaker: MLADJEN KENJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And before making the statement and talking to the Defence in August, on August 3rd, did you have a chance to review anything, any -- could have been any document, a diary, a prior statement you made, a prior statement someone else made? I mean, did you get a chance to do anything to refresh your recollection?

utterances.speaker: MLADJEN KENJIC
utterances.text: Well, the only statement that I gave earlier to OTP investigators was sometime in 2006.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness speak up a little, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you're not only invited to come closer to the microphone but also to speak a bit louder so that -- otherwise, your words will be lost which we would try to prevent to happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you have a chance to review that interview that you had in 2006?

utterances.speaker: MLADJEN KENJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you recall an interview you had in Sarajevo with the ICTY OTP people. It was on 16 March 2012 where, unlike the interview with Paul Grady of the OTP in 2006, you actually talked about some of the subjects that you have been talking about today?

utterances.speaker: MLADJEN KENJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, you changed the language of your question slightly. You said that you have had a chance to review that interview that you gave in 2006. Could you tell us when did you? Did you review that recently or before you gave the statement to Mr. Dundjer, or could you tell us when you reviewed that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, a day or two before. I didn't have the opportunity before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say "a day or two before." What? Before today? Or before you gave that statement to Mr. Dundjer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I only saw it yesterday. That first statement that I gave in 2006.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You did not see that or read that prior to your interview with Mr. Dundjer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed. Mr. McCloskey [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] but I have to switch on my microphone if I speak; it's unfortunately necessary. I invited you to proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Kenjic, I take it you do also remember the interview in Sarajevo with the OTP on -- in March 2012?

utterances.speaker: MLADJEN KENJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so -- we have a problem [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I notice it was only Mr. McCloskey's microphone that I could see was open. I now open mine. I close it again and see whether Mr. McCloskey's words will now reach the interpreters and then whether the words of the interpreters would reach us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So were you able to see a transcript of your March 2012 OTP interview before coming to court today?

utterances.speaker: MLADJEN KENJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And on your statement to the Defence of 3 August 2014, were you shown your OTP statement of March 2012 before giving that statement to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MLADJEN KENJIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't understand what you're asking. You're asking me about the first statement or the second one? I've seen both of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Focussing now on your statement to the Defence, we have thus far one statement, only one statement that you've given to the Defence. It's dated, as you've said, 3 August 2014. I'd like to know if you saw your OTP interview statement prior to giving your August 2013 [sic] statement to the Defence. 2014, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MLADJEN KENJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And prior to your 16 March 2012 interview with the OTP in Sarajevo, had the Defence team of General Mladic spoken to you?

utterances.speaker: MLADJEN KENJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So how many days before the OTP interview in Sarajevo on 16 March did you speak with the Mladic Defence?

utterances.speaker: MLADJEN KENJIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember. I cannot remember how many days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just roughly.

utterances.speaker: MLADJEN KENJIC
utterances.text: Two, three, five, seven, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who was that, that you spoke to, or that spoke to you?

utterances.speaker: MLADJEN KENJIC
utterances.text: Dundjer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And was Dundjer able to tell you a little bit about the information he would be asking you about?

utterances.speaker: MLADJEN KENJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, he must have told you something about what he was asking you about.

utterances.speaker: MLADJEN KENJIC
utterances.text: Maybe he told me, but I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, Witness, do you understand the English language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you take off your earphones for a second. Yes. Mr. McCloskey, I'm a bit confused. I think that we were talking now about Mr. Dundjer meeting with the witness before his OTP interview and you ask him what Mr. Dundjer said he would ask. Now that may be confusing, because usually you ask questions during an interview but it has not established there was an interview but just that they spoke a couple of days before the OTP interview. Now, of course, in the OTP interview I take it questions were put to him. So there may be some confusion as to questions being asked were you hinting at, whether Mr. Dundjer told what questions the OTP would ask him, or what questions he would ask him, although he would not interview him in the coming days. So I'm -- if I'm -- if the witness is as confused as I am, then please try to do something about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Kenjic, when you -- did you actually see Mr. Dundjer in person in those few days prior to giving an OTP interview?

utterances.speaker: MLADJEN KENJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Where did you meet with him?

utterances.speaker: MLADJEN KENJIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Where in Beograd?

utterances.speaker: MLADJEN KENJIC
utterances.text: At the office, the law firm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what did Mr. Dundjer say to you? What was the first thing he said to you about what this was all about?

utterances.speaker: MLADJEN KENJIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember what he said to me first. We talked, including about my coming here and my testimony, where I had been, what I had been doing, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And was he able to provide you a little information about General Mladic and -- and where he was and what he'd been doing?

utterances.speaker: MLADJEN KENJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But you spoke about where Mladic was during the period of 14, 15, 16 July with Mr. Dundjer that day.

utterances.speaker: MLADJEN KENJIC
utterances.text: Yes, we discussed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was there anybody else in the room with you and Mr. Dundjer during this discussion?

utterances.speaker: MLADJEN KENJIC
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't know. It's possible that there were people in other offices.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And getting into that 1995 time-frame, who was Mladic's other main driver? I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, if you would allow me to seek clarification. You told us that you met Mr. Dundjer in Belgrade a couple of days - three, four, five, six, seven days - before you were interviewed in Sarajevo. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now who took the initiative for that meeting? Did you call Mr. Dundjer? Did Mr. Dundjer call you? What happened that you met him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dundjer called me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And apart from talking about the whereabouts of Mr. Mladic, was Mr. Dundjer already aware that you would be interviewed a couple of days later in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Yes. It's -- therefore, is it pure coincidence that you happened to meet him just a couple of days you had this interview in Sarajevo in 2012?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Possibly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did you tell him that you were invited for an interview?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, in his office. I told him that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, to be fair, if you really think about it, you don't really know what Mr. Dundjer knew whether or not you were going to be interviewed by the OTP, do you?

utterances.speaker: MLADJEN KENJIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The only way you would have known what was in his head on that particular point would have been if he'd told you. In any event, I'll go on. In your statement, you told us who the other main driver for Mladic was in 1995. Can you remind us who that was?

utterances.speaker: MLADJEN KENJIC
utterances.text: Gojko Crnjak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And he had been Mladic's driver throughout the war, had he not been?

utterances.speaker: MLADJEN KENJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you had been -- you started driving regularly for General Mladic, what, in 1993?

utterances.speaker: MLADJEN KENJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. You've talked about the route you took on the 14th of July, after General Mladic wasn't able to get to Belgrade via helicopter and you finally left from Crna Rijeka. I want to show you a map of a couple of possible routes that we've picked out and see if you can identify if you took any of these routes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's 65 ter 33062.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: While this comes up, I would like to clarify one matter. Mr. McCloskey just asked you if you started driving regularly for General Mladic in 1993 and you said yes. In your statement, paragraph 2, you said this would start as of 18 May 1992. Which of the two is correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Both are correct. Both are correct. Because, in 1992, we travelled with two vehicles, two Puchs. I drove the escort, and the other one drove the boss. In 1993, that changed. I drove the general, and Gojko drove the others. It didn't really matter which one did which.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Maybe we can --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This, sir, is a map that we got from the Zvornik Brigade but to tell you that we added the yellow highlighting and we added the red highlighting that is noted as Route B. And if we could blow that up a bit more so hopefully you may be able to recognise ... In the bottom of the picture, we have -- let's blow up the bottom of the picture so we can see what city that is. Okay. So we see Han Pijesak there. And we see where the red and the yellow lines start. Is -- where the red and yellow lines start is that the approximate location of the Crna Rijeka headquarters of the VRS Main Staff? We can blow it up again if it will help.

utterances.speaker: MLADJEN KENJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. We see that it's right near this mountain called Veliki Zep. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's pan back so we that we can get a better picture of the route again. And -- yeah. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now we see the yellow route noted as Route A and the Route B is in red. And Route A goes through Vlasenica, Route B goes through Sekovici. You've said that -- you've testified that you took the regular route. Now, as you sit here now, do you remember which route you actually took, not just which route you normally took. But on that day, the afternoon of 14 July 1995, are you sure which route you took?

utterances.speaker: MLADJEN KENJIC
utterances.text: Quite.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Which one, if any of these?

utterances.speaker: MLADJEN KENJIC
utterances.text: Vlasenica, Milici, Zvornik, Karakaj, Sabac, Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. That would be the yellow route, Route A? And let's drop it down a little bit so we can get a little better picture of it. I'm sorry, let's blow it up a bit so we can start where the two routes verge from each other.

utterances.speaker: MLADJEN KENJIC
utterances.text: I told you clearly which route we took. I don't need to look at the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, that's just for our record so we're sure. So it's Route A. We see the route that goes up next to the Drina river and goes up past Zvornik to Karakaj?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Your answer, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Could we zoom in a bit more just to maybe get that blue arrow as it crosses Route A, the yellow route?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, just to go back a few lines. You said the one was the route through Vlasenica, the other was the route through --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sekovici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Sekovici. Is it true that it's in Vlasenica that the both split up and that the one goes through Milica and isn't it exactly -- and I'm trying to look at map and the word Han Pijesak we go to the north and there were -- what's the city? I read to the extent possible under red and yellow, Vlasenica, isn't it where they split up?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So both routes go through Vlasenica. The one, however, continues Sekovici and the other one, Milici.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because you said one was Vlasenica and the other was Sekovici but that's apparently not what you meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, that's -- thank you for clearing that up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So if we focus a bit on that blue arrow and without having to really read the map, that arrow is in the area between Nova Kasaba and Konjevic Polje. And were you aware at the time that on the 13th and 14th of July, large numbers of Muslim soldiers and civilians were fleeing the Srebrenica enclave and had crossed that road and were still in those woods all around that area where you're driving?

utterances.speaker: MLADJEN KENJIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Weren't you stopped at a check-point outside Nova Kasaba by the 65th Military Protection Regiment?

utterances.speaker: MLADJEN KENJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: As you drove past the Nova Kasaba area, did you see any large pits being dug near the side of the road?

utterances.speaker: MLADJEN KENJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When you got to Konjevic Polje, were you stopped at a MUP or army check-point, or any check-point?

utterances.speaker: MLADJEN KENJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when you were at Konjevic Polje, about how far were you from Kravica?

utterances.speaker: MLADJEN KENJIC
utterances.text: I don't understand that. What do you mean? As far as I know, Kravica is not on that road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, if you turn right and go towards Bratunac, it's about 9 kilometres from Konjevic Polje to Kravica, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MLADJEN KENJIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: At the time that you were in Konjevic Polje with General Mladic, did you have any information -- or did you hear any information that there were hundreds and hundreds of dead and dying Muslims at the Kravica warehouse at that time?

utterances.speaker: MLADJEN KENJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you drove northward along the road near the Drina. You went by the Jadar river, did you not?

utterances.speaker: MLADJEN KENJIC
utterances.text: Jadar sounds familiar, but I don't know where that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So I take it you didn't hear about any executions of 16 people, right near the road that you had driven by, that happened the day before, on the banks of the Jadar river?

utterances.speaker: MLADJEN KENJIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when you continued north that afternoon of the 14th and went by Zvornik, you actually drove right by the Zvornik Brigade headquarters in Karakaj, did you not?

utterances.speaker: MLADJEN KENJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, you drove by it, you didn't stop, I take it -- well, let me ask you. Did you drive by the headquarters or did you stop at the headquarters?

utterances.speaker: MLADJEN KENJIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes, yes. We passed by. We didn't stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when got to Karakaj, did you know that within about 8 kilometres to the east of Karakaj was a place called Orahovac where about 1.000 prisoners were in a school and were in the process of being murdered? Did you hear information about that when you were in Karakaj on the afternoon of 14 July?

utterances.speaker: MLADJEN KENJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So did you have any information about the other prisoners, roughly 800 to 1.000, at the nearby Petkovci school, the nearby Rocevic school, the Pilica cultural centre and the Kula school? Did you hear about any of those thousands of prisoners that were in those schools at the time that you're driving by that area?

utterances.speaker: MLADJEN KENJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go back so we see a bit more of the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I'm looking not at the map but at the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I -- yes, we should break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break of 20 minutes. We'd like to see you back after 20 minutes, Mr. Kenjic. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Kenjic, just on this map, we can make out Karakaj. It's not real clear but it is where the yellow and red routes meet, right near the Drina river. Is that where you crossed over on the bridge from Karakaj over to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MLADJEN KENJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And just lastly on this topic, when you were driving with General Mladic from Konjevic Polje through to Karakaj on the 14th of July, did you -- the Trial Chamber has heard the evidence that there were a very large number of buses and trucks and a large convoy taking thousands of Muslim men from Srebrenica along that route on the morning an afternoon hours of 14th July. Did you see any buses or trucks as you drove that very same route that very same day?

utterances.speaker: MLADJEN KENJIC
utterances.text: I didn't notice any kind of commotion on the road. It was as usual.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you -- I didn't ask you about commotion, did you see any buses or trucks with filled, with --

utterances.speaker: MLADJEN KENJIC
utterances.text: No, no. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would offer this map, 33062, into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 33062 receives exhibit number P7531, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P7531 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now let's go to 16 July. Let's look at your statement, D1218. I want to just take a quick look at paragraph 13, which should be on page 4 in the English and 4 in the B/C/S, and I just want to note that what you say in the middle of that paragraph and I quote: "I took the general and his wife home so that he could change and then I took them to the Military Medical Academy." And we can see from that paragraph that you're taking them home after the wedding festivity, you don't give any particular time for that. So let's look at your statement to the OTP on 16 March 2012, and that is 65 ter 32932. Should be English page 21, B/C/S page 30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You should perhaps ask the witness first if he remembers the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you have any recollection of about what time it was when you drove General Mladic and his wife from the restaurant festivities associated with the wedding to the apartment so they could change?

utterances.speaker: MLADJEN KENJIC
utterances.text: Around 6.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's look at your statement. You say that, near the bottom of the English, you're asked how long they stayed at the party and you say: "A long, long time." And then you were asked: "Did somebody from the wedding party bring out a drink for you?" And you said: "There was beer and coffee and cake, yes." Then you were asked: "Do you remember what time it was when you drove General Mladic to the next location?" And you say: "I didn't drive him anywhere else. I drove him home afterwards in the afternoon. I don't know what time it was. It might have been 3.00 or 4.00, as long as the lunch ceremony lasted. I don't know how long it lasted." Now you just answered 6.00. That's obviously --

utterances.speaker: MLADJEN KENJIC
utterances.text: Well, all right. I said it just like that, sort of afternoon, 6.00, 5.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You told the OTP 3.00 to 4.00. Now that you're testifying here, you're saying 6.00 and maybe 5.00. So you have been influenced between the time I told the OTP, 3.00 to 4.00 and what you're saying now, haven't you? Your recollection has been influenced in some way.

utterances.speaker: MLADJEN KENJIC
utterances.text: Oh, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's -- in paragraph 8 of your Defence statement, D1218, you say that General Mladic would sometimes arrive in Serbia by helicopter and that you would arrive by car and sometimes return him by car, vice versa. And there were times when General Mladic would arrive in Zvornik and you would go pick him up by car?

utterances.speaker: MLADJEN KENJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where would he land his helicopter in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: MLADJEN KENJIC
utterances.text: It didn't happen very often. That was during the ban on flights by NATO. He would come --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We didn't hear where.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and that would be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We weren't able -- the interpreters weren't able to make out where Mladic would actually land the helicopter during the NATO flight-ban time.

utterances.speaker: MLADJEN KENJIC
utterances.text: Drinjaca. It's this place towards Zvornik. There was a village stadium there on the river bank.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, that football pitch on the riverbank. That was near Milan Jolovic's apartment, Legenda's place, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MLADJEN KENJIC
utterances.text: That I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And in July 1995, was there a no-fly NATO ban for flying in Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MLADJEN KENJIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether there was a ban. Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And there was not a ban flying across Serbia at that time, was there?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please come closer to the microphone and speak up. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're invited to come closer to the microphone and to speak up.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so there wasn't a ban in -- a flight ban in Serbia in July 1995, was there?

utterances.speaker: MLADJEN KENJIC
utterances.text: How could I know that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, you were driving the general of the VRS across Serbia, across the RS. That's why you would know, isn't it? Isn't that a good enough reason?

utterances.speaker: MLADJEN KENJIC
utterances.text: I didn't drive a helicopter. I drove a automobile.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What was the name of Mladic's main helicopter pilot? You've told us this before.

utterances.speaker: MLADJEN KENJIC
utterances.text: I don't know the name, but it's Mara.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's Maran or Mara?

utterances.speaker: MLADJEN KENJIC
utterances.text: Maran.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that's Dusan Maran; correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADJEN KENJIC
utterances.text: Possibly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what did General Mladic call him?

utterances.speaker: MLADJEN KENJIC
utterances.text: Well, believe me, I don't know. Now did he call him Maran or Dule, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, go back in the war years. He called him Dule, didn't he? His nickname, a classic nickname for Dusan.

utterances.speaker: MLADJEN KENJIC
utterances.text: Possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to 65 ter 33060. This is an OTP interview of Mr. Crnjak, the other driver. Let's go page 16 in English, pages 22 and 23 in the B/C/S. Should be about the middle of the page. And we can see there were -- on that page they're talking about pilot and Mr. Blaszczyk asked: "Do you remember the pilot's name?" And Crnjak says: "Dule, Maran, I think, yes." And then Mr. Blaszczyk says: "Could Dule be Dusan?" And he says: "I don't know, something like that?" Does that help refresh your recollection that your fellow driver remembered Dule?

utterances.speaker: MLADJEN KENJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to 65 ter 32931. This is an interview of Dusan Maran. Page 9 in the English; page 9 in the B/C/S. And down at the bottom of the page, Mr. Maran in answer to a question says: "Sometimes I would not even see him, but his escort would come, or sometimes [sic] else from the staff" -- excuse me, "... someone else from the staff whom I knew, whom I had met or seen to tell me: Dule, go to ... point A, pick up three passengers, or go get the wounded and take him to another hospital." So, this would be Mr. Maran referring to himself as Dule, would it not?

utterances.speaker: MLADJEN KENJIC
utterances.text: How could I know that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, that's what it is. Does that help refresh your recollection as to his nickname?

utterances.speaker: MLADJEN KENJIC
utterances.text: It doesn't mean a thing to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to Exhibit P1656. This is a ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Not to be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, sir, this is an intercepted conversation where the Muslim security services have provided an intercept between General Mladic and someone called Dule, and it is dated 16 July at 0830 hours in the morning. And Dule says: "It's Dule." Mladic says: "I'll see you tonight, Dule." Dule says: "Fine." Mladic says: "Bye." So you were with General Mladic for some time on the 16th of July, including in the evening, in Belgrade. Are you aware of General Mladic meeting anyone named Dule the night of 16 July in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MLADJEN KENJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you now of him meeting Mladic, a Dule Maran meeting Mladic in Zvornik or Belgrade on the 16th, on the evening?

utterances.speaker: MLADJEN KENJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you ever travel in a helicopter with General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MLADJEN KENJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you get into a helicopter on the night of the 16th at the heli-pad at the VMA and go with General Mladic to Zvornik, to the pitch near Zvornik and then drive him to Crna Rijeka?

utterances.speaker: MLADJEN KENJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. One last reference to the interview of Mr. Crnjak, the other driver, 65 ter 33060. Should be pages 13 and 14 in English; 18 and 19 in the B/C/S. And Mr. Blaszczyk again, asking Mr. Crnjak: "Did you ever get the opportunity to travel with him to Belgrade by helicopter?" Meaning General Mladic. And Crnjak said: "Yes, I did." Blaszczyk says: "Where? Later on, you drove another vehicle as a driver?" And Crnjak says: "Yes." And then Erin Gallagher says: "So you travelled with him by helicopter." And Crnjak says: "Yes, several times." So Crnjak, a regular driver like yourself, acknowledges that he travels several times with General Mladic in helicopter. How so that you say that you never travelled with him by helicopter?

utterances.speaker: MLADJEN KENJIC
utterances.text: Never. Really, never. If you understood what I said. Really, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I have nothing further, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Fluegge has one or more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to take you back to the day when you escorted or drove Mr. Mladic to the church where the wedding took place. Where did you meet Mr. Mladic after the wedding next?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I picked him up in front of the restaurant. That same day, when that wedding took place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: How far was the restaurant away from the church?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know, but, believe me, they went on foot, so I assume that it's not very far away from the church to the restaurant. They walked and I followed them in the car.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: If you followed them by the car, you should be able to give us an approximate distance.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let's say, 500 metres. Maybe a bit more; maybe a bit less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would also have a question for you. Let me just first check on the transcript. Yes, you said today that on any other vehicle than the Puch there was no equipment, and you specified no radio equipment and you specified that that was true for the Ford Taunus as well. In your statement, I read - and perhaps we could have it on our screen, D1218, paragraph 11; I think with the cover page, it's the third page. Could we have the B/C/S version as well. Yes, there you say: "As far as I remember, we headed for Serbia in a civilian Ford Taunus that did not have any special communications equipment ..." Did it have any communications equipment, any normal communications equipment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, none.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What could you explain why you used the wording "special communications equipment"? Because if there's none at all why would you say there was no special equipment? Why wouldn't you say there was no communications equipment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I really don't know why I put it that way, but I know that we did not have any kind of communications in these cars, or in that car, except in the Puch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say in your statement, as far as you remember, you apparently are not sure about it. Is that well understood.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Quite. I assert that there was no communication that we had in that car.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You did not correct that when you reviewed your statement by saying, It's not whether I remember or not, but it's just a firm fact that I state about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, possibly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Possibly what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that, that I didn't change that in my statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You didn't change anything in your statement, and the first draft stayed as it was when it was presented to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't think I would have changed anything except for all this that I said in that statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was it on the day of the statement, the interview is on the 3rd of August. Was -- on that same day, was the first draft presented to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When was it -- how long after the interview was the draft statement given to you for review?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean this version, this statement that I gave to the lawyer? I only saw it yesterday, the day before yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you signed it last year, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, my question was: Was it on the same day that you were interviewed that you were given the draft statement for review after which you said nothing has to be changed? Was it the same day or was it another day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, it was on the same day. I signed it on the same day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And was it -- was there a pause between your interview and their preparing the statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really cannot remember if there had been a break or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have any recollection as to how they wrote this down? You say, I don't know whether there was a break. Or was there already a draft prepared at the beginning of the interview and that you went through that and then signed it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He put questions to me, I answered, and I suppose that's the way they formulated it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But what was written on paper, do you have any recollection as whether they had prepared something already or whether they took the time after the interview, whether there was -- how did this happen? Or did they write it down during the interview, or was it immediately given to you for signature or first for review? Could you tell us a bit more what you remember from that interview in this respect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We talked, and when we finished that conversation, then they put it down on paper. I signed it. And that was it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You were present when they put it down on paper?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How long did that take approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stojanovic, any questions in re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have no further questions for this witness. I just want to thank Mr. Kenjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kenjic, this concludes your testimony in this court because the Defence has no further questions for you, and, therefore, there's no room for Mr. McCloskey to put any further questions to you. I'd like to thank you very much for coming a long way to The Hague and for answering all the questions that were put to you, put to you by the parties, put to you by the Bench. I wish you a safe return home again. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, do I understand that there are no witnesses available for the remainder of this week?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, you understand correctly. This is the second week, we had the same problem with the same witness, and we will -- we are not going to call that witness in the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are not going to the call the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... VWS that he does not feel well and that he cannot testify in this case. So we cannot call him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, I leave it to you whether you consider that he is unable to come or not. But you remove --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Our decision is final.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your decision is final.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, we are removing him from the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you repeat his name. He's not protected, is he?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: He is not protected. His name is Mr. Kesar Ostoja [phoen].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kesar, and that's hereby put on the record, is removed with our leave from the 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we have still some time left. I'd like to use that deal with a few procedural matters before we adjourn and that would be an adjournment until Monday, because your next witness is available to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Our next witness is available on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I ... Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Also to let you know, I've spoken with Mr. Lukic about an another -- we can call it a procedural matter. It was a question you had of us back in March regarding the Pelemisi testimony and Mr. Pelemis and I can, of course, try to take us through that. We've been able to answer some of your questions and discuss that a bit with the Defence. If you would like, we can do that in open court or in some other manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How much time would it ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If Mr. McCloskey just mentions the exhibit number, we would withdraw our objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, I best help refresh everyone's recollection if you want to go through that so we can -- because it's a little more complicated than that but I do appreciate the withdrawal but I'm not sure any of us will remember what we are talking about. It took me a while to figure this out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To be quite honest, I have got no idea Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And perhaps I should be ashamed to admit it. But it is for a fact. Perhaps I do understand that you fear that Mr. Lukic has no idea either about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: He actually does. We were able to have some coffee over it and he has obviously come to some conclusion and I hope if all a bit vague we can then present you with documents and transcripts and all that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Would it be good -- would it be a good idea that you briefly - apparently you have discussed the matter - that you set out, both parties together, what exactly the issue was and what now the results are. We read that and then put on the record whatever has to be put on the record. Is that brief introduction in writing informal submission? Is that something, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand. You want us to make a verbal informal discussion or paper? We're fine with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it's a matter of a few minutes then let's deal with it in open court. If it takes more time we'd rather have an informal introduction. Or just we are referring to this-and-this issue and then we'll find out and then we'll hear what the result is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If I can take probably a minute to set the scene for you and you probably then either want to say, enough, send me paper or no, we're beginning to remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One minute is a fair offer, isn't it, Mr. Lukic. One minute you have, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Pelemis was testifying about the events in 1992 related to Pelemisi. I had an UN report, it was 65 ter 11377, a commission of expert report that had a section about Kladanj. We were talking about some sexual assaults that happened in this little village of Pelemisi. When I read that section of the expert report referring to sexual assault allegations, it was clear that there was footnoted, this paragraph in the report was footnoted, and you had asked what the footnotes were, and so we have, for the last several months, been trying to sort out what those footnotes were and we finally figured it out, and we have about two pages of the material that the footnote is based upon. Now I offered the little section on Kladanj of the expert report into evidence, and Mr. Lukic objected to that, and then we all agreed that it would be best before you made a decision on that section to be able to get an idea of what the footnotes were about. So I now have two pages that are reference to the footnote which I gave to Mr. Lukic yesterday and naturally we would like to give you the fullest picture possible, the two or three pages of footnotes as well as the section, the small paragraph on Kladanj. I believe Mr. Lukic has agreed that the small section on Kladanj referring to the sexual assaults can come into evidence. My guess is he might have something else to say about the footnotes. And since, Your Honour, you asked about the footnotes we have them, of course, for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We would leave Your Honours to decide whether footnotes should be included or not. But [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... we are not objecting to that small Kladanj portion from the expert report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you object to have the footnotes, if tendered, to be admitted? The footnote material.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I leave it to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, is it that you wish to tender the footnote material? We haven't seen it so I've got no idea at this moment. You said that there's two pages?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. What we have is a little packet that shows the first page of the UN report that will help us maybe remember what the report is from. The table of contents, you get an idea of what the report is about. The paragraph on Kladanj, just the one page and then the two -- actually three pages of footnotes and the reference, so that we can see the footnote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I suggest the following. If you upload this - I don't know whether it's uploaded already as a 65 ter - and you tender that package as a whole and there's no objection from the Defence, if I understand Mr. Lukic well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then it would be 65 ter number -- you may have mentioned it already.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's 11377a now because it has the complete packet for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's marked for identification. We'll have a look at it and then decide on admission.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And it was from transcript 33830 back in March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That certainly will help us in preparing our decision on admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could you already assign the number for 11377a.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This receives exhibit number P7532, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And it's 7532 that is marked for identification. And we'll, in due course decide on admission. Having dealt with that, I will deal with a few other procedural matters. First, remaining issue from the testimony of Tomislav Savkic. During his testimony on the 22nd of October of last year, 2014, D705, a notebook entry allegedly written by Izet Redzic was marked for identification following the Prosecution's objection to its admission on the grounds that Savkic could not confirm whether he ever saw the original of the document or whether it had been added to later on. I refer to transcript pages 27140, 41 and 149, 50. On the 22nd of October of that same year, the Prosecution further disputed the authenticity of the date on the document and the document's probative value. Transcript page 27211. The Chamber also invited the parties to agree on the text of illegible parts of the document and that's two and three pages further down in the transcript. In an e-mail dated the 10th of December of 2014 that the handwritten number at the top of the document reads 12 instead of 16. The Defence informed the Chamber in an e-mail on the 11th of February, 2015 that a revised English translation had been uploaded into e-court under doc ID 1D19-1247, but that remaining legibility issues needed to be resolved with the Prosecution. According to the Prosecution, it provided the Defence with another revised English translation on the 20th of March of 2015. The Chamber has sent ten e-mails since December 2014 regarding the parties' progress. On 29th of June and 3rd of August of this year, the Chamber asked whether the revised English translation from the 20th of March, 2015 had been uploaded into e-court and what its doc ID was. On the 3rd of August, the Prosecution responded that it had not uploaded the translation. The Defence has not responded. The Chamber denies the admission of D705 without prejudice. I now will deal with the remaining issue from the testimony of Mladen Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I just may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please. If the Prosecution sends something for translation we cannot upload it. And if it's not our fault that it's not uploaded, only the Prosecution can upload it if they send it for translation. There must be some reason why they send it for translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now you have not --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... I don't know it by heart now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it's without prejudice if you do not respond to such a request whether it's uploaded or not because it was your document. If the translation is not there, I would have expected you to inform the Chamber that you did not receive a proper translation and that was the reason why you couldn't upload it and then we might have decided differently. But it's without prejudice. The ruling is there. You may revisit the matter --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- if you consider that wise. And, at this moment, I'll not pay further attention to whether the Prosecution should have provided another translation to the Defence. I leave that apart from this moment. But that's why we invite parties to make submissions, Mr. Lukic, that we are fully informed and not informed after we have ruled on a matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We saw recently, Your Honour, that we have a problem with following all those e-mails and we have already suffered grave consequences in regard of some of the rulings. So it is really hard for the Defence to follow everything that comes through e-mails to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. These are usually reminders of what was dealt with in court. Let's not forget that. And, second, if there's any problem there, if you need more time, then you can always ask for it. Whether we give it or not is another matter but that's the appropriate way. And perhaps you should have someone who closely follows whatever requests are sent by the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The problem is we have no one. That's the problem. We don't have enough people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just to keep track of that would take me --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If it's the only thing it would be easy for us but we have so much to do so we really have a problem with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would give priority at least of what the Chamber asks for information. Let's not discuss it at this moment. I move on to the remaining issues from the testimony of Mladen Blagojevic. On the 5th of March of this year, during the testimony of Mladen Blagojevic, Exhibit P7187 was reserved for an extract of the first video of an interview with the witness dated the 15th of October, 2004. This can be found at transcript pages 32662 through 663. On the 26th of August, the Prosecution notified the Chamber and the Defence via an e-mail that the parties had agreed on the admission of, one, the entire first video along with its CLSS revised translation which bears Rule 65 ter number 32112a and two, an excerpt of the second video of the interview which bears Rule 65 ter number 32155a. The Chamber hereby instructs the Registry to attach Rule 65 ter number 32112a to exhibit number P7187 and admits it into evidence. The Chamber further admits Rule 65 ter number 32155a into evidence but, Madam Registrar, would you please assign a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 32155a receives exhibit number P7533, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. I will now deliver the Chamber's decision on a Defence motion to amend its Rule 65 ter witness list. On the 28th of July, 2015, the Defence filed a motion to amend its Rule 65 ter witness list to add one witness. On the 7th of August, the Prosecution filed its response, not objecting to the motion. The Defence submits that due to medical reasons, the witness was not identified as a witness in its 19th of May, 2014 Rule 65 ter filing. Further, the Defence submits that even if this does not amount to a showing of good cause, it is in the interests of justice to grant the motion as the witness provides relevant and probative evidence crucial to the Defence case. The Chamber recalls and refers to the applicable law regarding additions to the Defence witness list, as set out in its decision dated the 12th of August, 2014 on the Defence motion to amend witness list. With regard to the Defence's arguments that good cause exists for not having identified the witness at an earlier stage, the Chamber notes that the medical documentation presented in support of the Defence submission does not substantiate the Defence's claim that this proposed witness could not be interviewed before the filing of the Rule 65 ter witness list. The Chamber notes that the Rule 65 ter witness list predates the treatment detailed in the medical documentation. Also, the medical documentation does not include any information about the existence of any medical problems for this witness as at the time of the Rule 65 ter filing. Therefore, the Chamber finds that the Defence has failed to demonstrate good cause for not including this witness on the list. Nonetheless, the Chamber considers the anticipated evidence of this witness as outlined in the motion, to be prima facie relevant and of probative value. Furthermore, the Prosecution did not oppose the addition of this witness to the Defence's witness list. In light of the foregoing, the Chamber considers that it is in the interests of justice to grant the Defence' 28 July 2015 motion and instructs the Defence to provide the relevant information for this witness pursuant to Rule 65 ter (G)(i) within ten days of the date of this decision. I would briefly like to turn into private session for one remaining item before we adjourn for the day.
